Course Description:
This course covers analytical tools and topics that have not been discussed in previous
operations doctoral courses at Yale SOM. The emphasis is on approaches to modeling
and analyzing operational processes across various application areas, including supply
chains, service operations, retail operations, platform operations, and sustainable
operations. Students will explore key ideas and methodologies established in the
literature of Operations Research and Operations Management, understand the contexts
in which certain conventions have been developed, and learn how to build effective
mathematical models.  Part-1 and Part-2 can be taken independently. Students can enroll in both or only one.
faculty_bio: Uri Simonsohn is a Visiting Professor of Behavioral Science at Yale School of Management for the 2026–27 academic year and a Professor of Behavioral Science at ESADE Business School in Barcelona. His research focuses on judgment and decision-making, research methods, and the credibility and reproducibility of empirical findings. He teaches topics related to motivating behavioral change and improving people’s understanding of data through psychological research. Before joining ESADE, he was a professor at the Wharton School, where he served from 2003 to 2017. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/uri-simonsohn))

Course Description:
This course covers a wide range of models of operational processes with focus on physical
goods, which means that the course will not have much coverage of service processes.
Example of types of issues covered are key assumptions and setups, deterministic vs
uncertain demand, trade-off between too much and two little, short life-cycle products
vs long-term products with replenishment, multi-locations, vertical vs horizontal pricing,
delayed differentiation and modular product architecture, centralized and decentralized
decision making, bayesian updating of information and its influence on decisions.
faculty_bio: Nils Rudi is a Professor of Operations Management and Professor of Statistics and Data Science at Yale School of Management, where he earned his PhD from The Wharton School in 2000. His research focuses on managing uncertainty in supply chains and applying data-driven methods across areas including sports analytics, cognitive psychology, education, health care, and law. He teaches probability modeling, operational-process modeling, sports analytics, and a Yale Law School course on uncertainty, data, and judgment. Before academia, Rudi worked as a computer programmer and founded Minard, a decision-support company for forecasting and inventory management; he previously taught at the University of Rochester and INSEAD. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/nils-rudi))

Course Description: This is a short course on the theory and practice of leading, managing, and functioning in task-performing groups and teams. It has two primary goals: first, to provide students with a conceptual framework for analyzing group dynamics, diagnosing performance problems, and designing appropriate interventions, and second, to help students develop practical skills for building effective groups and teams. Both of these objectives are important to students’ effectiveness in study groups at SOM and in organizational teams they will join or lead after graduation. The design of the course is based on the belief that conceptual understanding of the principles of team effectiveness is of little use without a more direct experiential understanding of group dynamics (or process) and the behavioral skills required to implement this knowledge. This one-week course takes place the week following orientation. Course session times will be announced in Canvas.
Daytimes: M T W Th F 8:30 AM-4:30 PM
faculty_bio: Julia DiBenigno is a Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management, with a courtesy appointment in Sociology. An organizational ethnographer and field researcher, she studies the sociology of work and occupations, collaboration across professional groups, upward influence and voice, and organizational change; she also teaches Managing Groups and Teams. Her background includes a PhD and MS from MIT Sloan, a summa cum laude psychology degree from Columbia, and prior consulting work in Deloitte’s Organization and Change practice. Course Description: The course helps students acquire basic accounting knowledge that is extremely useful in the day-to-day practice of general management. This basic accounting knowledge is indispensable background for the work to follow in the Organizational Perspectives courses as well as for elective courses in accounting, finance, marketing, and strategy. Accounting systems provide important financial information for all types of organizations across the globe. Despite their many differences, all accounting systems are built on a common foundation. Economic concepts, such as assets, liabilities, and income, are used to organize information into a fairly standard set of financial statements. Bookkeeping mechanics compile financial information with the double entry system of debits and credits. Accounting conventions help guide the application of the concepts through the mechanics. This course provides these fundamentals of accounting.
faculty_bio: Anya Nakhmurina is an Associate Professor of Accounting at the Yale School of Management. Her research examines the information environment of U.S. municipalities, especially financial-reporting transparency, municipal disclosures, governance, public finance, and cities’ climate-change adaptation and mitigation decisions. She earned a PhD in Accounting from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and is an Affiliate Fellow of Booth’s Stigler Center for the Study of the Economy and the State. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/anya-nakhmurina))

Course Description: The ability to understand and apply probability concepts and statistical methods is fundamental to management education. The concepts covered in this course include probability, simulation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and applied regression modeling. This course provides a foundation of basic statistical concepts that are essential for many other courses at SOM. These materials surface routinely in students’ Organizational Perspectives courses and electives and are useful for decision-making applications in financial analysis, marketing, operations management, and other areas.
faculty_bio: Seth Zimmerman is the Eli and Edythe Broad Professor of Economics, Education, and Management at Yale School of Management and faculty research director of The Broad Center. His research focuses on labor economics, public finance, and the economics of education, including educational attainment, returns to education, upward mobility, inequality, and school-choice policy. He earned his PhD, MPhil, and MA from Yale University and his BA from Dartmouth College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/seth-zimmerman))

Course Description: This course concentrates on the role of market processes in determining the opportunities facing individuals and business firms, the policy issues facing public officials, and the patterns of resource allocation in the economic system. It is intended to be accessible to students with little or no prior exposure to economics. The mathematical prerequisite is competence with basic algebra and calculus. The aim is to provide students with analytical tools to help them tackle economic problems, which arise whenever agents must make economic trade-offs or engage in trade. While we cover a range of topics in microeconomics, the emphasis throughout the course is on learning how to approach and tackle economic problems—a skill that will be useful in making managerial decisions. Topics include supply and demand, consumers, production, equilibrium, imperfect competition, competitive strategy.
faculty_bio: Kai Hao Yang is an Associate Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. His research uses mechanism design and information design to study privacy, algorithmic fairness, price discrimination, consumer data, online platforms, political economy, and finance; he also teaches economics courses at Yale SOM. He earned a B.A. in Political Science from National Taiwan University and an M.A. and Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Chicago, and was previously a postdoctoral associate at Yale’s Cowles Foundation. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kai-hao-yang))

Course Description:
This course is designed for students seeking a decisive competitive advantage by mastering the ability to both deploy and build custom AI agents for the modern enterprise. While the AI landscape is fast-evolving, the primary differentiator for future leaders is the transition from being a passive consumer of AI to an architect of AI-driven solutions.

The curriculum provides a rigorous, hands-on environment focused on fundamental, general-purpose AI building skills. Students move from theoretical understanding to the practical construction of tools using vibe coding and agentic frameworks. By the end of the thirteen sessions, students will have developed the technical intuition and engineering skills to build AI agents that integrate APIs, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), tool use, and autonomous workflows—skills that transfer across business functions and domains.
faculty_bio: Tauhid Zaman is an Associate Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management, where he also serves as Lecturer in Management and Special Advisor for AI Initiatives. His research uses probabilistic models, network algorithms, and modern statistical methods to address operational problems involving social-network data, including content popularity, online extremism, and user geolocation. He also studies data-driven startup investing, choice modeling, algorithmic sports betting, and biometric data. Zaman earned his BS, MEng, and PhD in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT, completing his doctorate in 2011. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tauhid-zaman))

Course Description:
This course is designed for students seeking a decisive competitive advantage by mastering the ability to both deploy and build custom AI agents for the modern enterprise. While the AI landscape is fast-evolving, the primary differentiator for future leaders is the transition from being a passive consumer of AI to an architect of AI-driven solutions.

The curriculum provides a rigorous, hands-on environment focused on fundamental, general-purpose AI building skills. Students move from theoretical understanding to the practical construction of tools using vibe coding and agentic frameworks. By the end of the thirteen sessions, students will have developed the technical intuition and engineering skills to build AI agents that integrate APIs, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), tool use, and autonomous workflows—skills that transfer across business functions and domains.
faculty_bio: Tauhid Zaman is an Associate Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management, where he also serves as Lecturer in Management and Special Advisor for AI Initiatives. Course Description:
Why do some people move up the economic ladder while others do not? How do education, family background, labor markets, public policy, and technology shape economic opportunity?
This course examines inequality and social mobility in the United States and around the world through a data-driven lens. We will study how income, wealth, race, gender, geography, education, labor-market institutions, and technological change influence economic opportunity and the distribution of resources across generations. Topics include intergenerational mobility, segregation, education, taxation and redistribution, globalization, the future of work, and the role of firms and public institutions in expanding opportunity.
Drawing on frontier economic research and empirical case studies, students will learn to evaluate evidence, assess competing explanations for economic disparities, and analyze policies designed to promote opportunity. AI will be integrated throughout the course as a tool for research, analysis, and communication, while also serving as a lens through which to examine the future of work and economic mobility.
Course Title: Inequality and Social Mobility: Understanding Opportunity in the Age of AI
faculty_bio: Barbara Biasi is an Associate Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. Course Description:
Interpersonal influence isn’t rocket science but it’s a science. It’s not magic but as you learn to apply the science it’ll sometimes feel like a superpower. In this course, you’ll study influence strategies that feel comfortable on both sides so that you can be persuasive without being manipulative. Drawing on research from social psychology, behavioral economics, and neuroscience, you’ll be deepening your knowledge through readings and class discussions, then conducting your own experiments in real-world challenges. Your synthesis of knowledge and practice will leave you better equipped to get job offers, fund startups, collaborate with teams, negotiate deals, influence policies, smooth disagreements, improve your relationships, amplify your activism, and connect with people.

We do a lot in 7 weeks! You’ll hit the ground running with deliverables due Mon/Wed/Fri, beginning immediately. Expect readings, challenges, and deliverables to take 5-10h/week. You’ll also participate in an evening challenge and publish an article. And if you put in the effort, you’ll have fun and make some friends :-)

Set the stage for achieving your goals through ongoing mastery of influence and persuasion in a boot camp-style intensive course. Help you become a person people increasingly want to say yes to.    Whether you have formal authority or not, your effectiveness as a leader and change agent depends on your ability to influence others to want to follow you. To want to say Yes. In this boot camp practicum, you'll study research findings and discuss tools like handling resistance and using other people's standards for themselves, but the real work and real benefit happens outside of class. You'll put influence into practice with weekly G-Force challenges to help you gain useful skills, shift your thinking, and build resilience. Although you'll learn some red flags to watch out for so you can protect yourself against would-be manipulators, and we'll discuss how to handle difficult people, we focus on making influence more comfortable and fun for all parties. Because then you'll be more likely to use it. Which means you'll be a stronger leader, better able to shape the world around you. Research shows nice people DO finish first—but ""nice"" might be different from what you thought. 

Find out for yourself.

Course Description: This course offers students the opportunity to develop skills and acquire experience in dealing with strategic marketing problems. The course aimes at helping students look at the entire marketing mix in light of the strategy of the firm. The course builds on the foundation developed in core courses, and the basic framework rests on the recent development in economics and strategy – resource based view (RBV) of strategy. You will have a chance to illustrate your ability to apply this framework in this course through case discussion and an in-class final exam. It will be most helpful to students pursuing careers in which they need to look at the firm as a whole. Examples include consultants, investment analysts, entrepreneurs, and product managers. Case studies will highlight marketing strategy exercise in consumer packaged goods, high tech, pharmaceuticals, and luxury goods.

Course description: This course will be co-taught by Jeffrey E. Garten and Robert D. Hormats, whose combined experience spans the Nixon, Ford, Carter, Reagan, Clinton, and Obama administrations, as well as decades on Wall Street. The course is based on the premise that America's role and policies in the global economy are undergoing a profound change that will outlast the current administration in Washington. It will examine the major forces in the U.S. and abroad that will be determining America's future in the global economy and the likely policies it will follow for the next decade. These will include changes in the country's industrial and financial structures, new social pressures, new demographic patterns, and evolving political alignments. Typical of the kinds of questions to be examined will be: How will the changing labor force affect America's interest in the global arena? How will changing technology affect these interests? What about changes in energy and the environment? What will trade policy, policy toward foreign investment and immigration policy look like? How should we think about the changing roles of Wall Street, Corporate America, and Silicon Valley? Regarding developments abroad, we will ask questions such as these: How will China's evolving interests, or new directions for the European Union, or the changing position of big emerging markets, or new pressures in global finance influence American policy, and with what effect? If the U.S. attempts to reduce its international involvement, who will write and try to enforce the "rules of the game?" Given the centrality of the United States to the global economy, the course will be important global background for future leaders in any profession. SEE SYLLABUS.
faculty_bio: Jeffrey E. His teaching focuses on global finance and global business, including financial centers, China’s role in the global economy, and leading multinational companies. Before joining Yale, Garten was U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade and spent 13 years on Wall Street, including roles at Lehman Brothers and the Blackstone Group. He holds a PhD and MA from Johns Hopkins University and a BA from Dartmouth College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jeffrey-e-garten))

Policy modeling refers to applications of operations research and allied quantitative methods to policy problems. Policy modeling is most useful when the amounts of data, money, time, and other resources one would like for purely scientific investigation are highly constrained by the decision-making environment. Recognizing that analyses of all sorts often exhibit diminishing returns in insight to effort, the idea is to capture key features of various policy issues with relatively simple "first-strike" models that provide support for decision making. Building on earlier coursework in probability modeling, this course introduces a toolkit of such models, including optimization, cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness analysis, Bernoulli processes, hazard and duration models, random incidence, Markov models, queueing and fluid models, and algorithms—and shows how to apply them to policy questions.
The course will feature applications to problems drawn from public health, criminal justice, public housing, education, and other areas of public policy. Students will be responsible for attending all classes and participating in class discussions. There will be problem sets, which must be submitted on time to receive credit, and a few short in-class quizzes (see the syllabus for details). There is NO final exam. 
Prerequisite: Students must have completed MGT 403 (Probability Modeling and Statistics) or equivalent to take this class. The probability modeling knowledge required is covered in any introductory probability course and includes: sample space, event probabilities including marginal, joint and conditional, Bayes' Rule, random variables, probability distributions, expected value, mean, variance, Bernoulli, binomial, uniform, and normal random variables, independence, covariance and correlation, and sums of random variables (both independent and dependent). Policy modeling is not a class in statistics or econometrics.

She earned a Ph.D. in Management Science and Engineering from Stanford University and was a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University. Course Description:
This is not your usual start-up course. This is a course about how to be entrepreneurial in reducing health disparities and achieving public health goals. This includes both non-profit and for-profit entrepreneurship; and intrapreneurship, which means innovating within existing institutions (government agencies, non-profits, for-profits). We also focus heavily on extrapreneurship, which is the idea of innovating across the boundaries of multiple institutions.

The course is centered on health equity, which means that everyone has a fair and just opportunity to be as healthy as possible. This requires addressing obstacles to health such as poverty, racism, gender and other biases and their consequences; including disparities in power, livelihood, education, housing, food, safety, and health care services. We refer to these as drivers of health. Across careers and professions, our work influences and is influenced by one or more drivers of health.

In this case-based course, we examine a wide spectrum of public health entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship (PHEI) cases ranging from collective action in a non-profit setting to digital start-ups in a venture-backed setting. This course brings together students from the Schools of Management, Public Health, Environment, Global Affairs, Divinity, Engineering, Arts and Sciences, and undergraduates. There are no prerequisites, all are welcome.
faculty_bio: Teresa Chahine is a Senior Lecturer in Social Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management and Faculty Director of the Social Innovation Initiative at Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs. She teaches social entrepreneurship and researches tools for advancing social and environmental determinants of health, including how to finance, measure, and scale social impact. Chahine previously launched a public-health entrepreneurship program at Harvard and founded Lebanon’s first venture-philanthropy organization. She is also the author of *Social Entrepreneurship: Building Impact Step by Step*. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/teresa-chahine))

Course Description: Most of you will spend 80% of your career as part of a team. In this highly interactive course, you will learn the theory and practice of leading, managing, and performing in task-oriented teams. Through weekly in-class exercises that simulate the challenges encountered by real-world groups and leaders, you will develop a conceptual understanding of group dynamics, experience these dynamics firsthand, and develop practical skills to support team effectiveness. You will leave with a better understanding of how to create structures and environments to help your teams make high-quality decisions, produce innovative solutions to problems, complete their projects in a timely and efficient manner, while supporting the development and experience of individual team members.
faculty_bio: David M. Munguia Gomez is an Assistant Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management. His research examines how people allocate rewards and opportunities—such as college admission and employment—with particular attention to ethical tensions involving merit, circumstance, and disadvantage, using experiments, surveys, and interviews. He earned a PhD in behavioral science from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and an AB in psychology from Princeton University, and his research has appeared in leading management and psychology journals and received best paper awards. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/david-m-munguia-gomez))

Course Description:
In this course, we will explore how to drive growth in emerging consumer-facing ventures. Through case studies, frameworks, and practical applications, students will examine how to win the hearts and minds and open the wallets of consumers while profitably scaling through an agile, test-and-learn approach.

Key objectives:

• Understand the building blocks of a high-performing growth strategy.

• Analyze unit economics (LTV and CAC) and key drivers of profitability.

• Navigate advertising channels, media mix strategies, and measurement approaches.

• Develop creative testing and conversion optimization tactics.

• Leverage CRM tools and tactics to build customer loyalty and community.

• Create effective content and partnerships to amplify brand reach.

• Design an integrated growth campaign and define success metrics.

Students will gain actionable insights for entrepreneurial growth strategies and deeper understanding of growth marketing frameworks also applicable to larger consumer-facing enterprises.
faculty_bio: Laura Jones (LJ) Joukovski is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management, where she teaches Direct-to-Consumer Entrepreneurship. Her focus is on the practical challenges of building and scaling consumer brands, including strategy, marketing, finance, operations, and organizational leadership. She is CEO of DFTBA, a board member, investor, and advisor, and previously served as CEO of JustFab and helped scale brands including Fabletics and Savage X Fenty. Joukovski holds an MBA from Yale SOM and a BS in Economics from Davidson College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/laura-joukovski))

Course Description:
The purpose of this course is to provide students with an opportunity to explore being an entrepreneur by purchasing a company, rather than starting one from scratch. The readings and class discussions will help students understand how to purchase a business, finance an acquisition, and operate and grow a business. The cases and conversations will help students understand what it is like being a young, first time CEO and what types of challenges and issues will be encountered.
The general course structure will follow the lifecycle of an entrepreneur who purchases a business to operate. The first few session will explore the concept of entrepreneurship through acquisition and how this compares to different forms of entrepreneurship and its pros and cons. How to purchase a business and what type of business to purchase will be examined. How to operate and grow a business as a young, first time CEO will be considered. What happens when a business works well and when it does not work well will be discussed. Finally, how and when to sell a business and what that means for the entrepreneur and business will be reviewed. This course will require active participation in class. Please be prepared and committed to participate in class. If you do not enjoy participating in class, this might not be the right course for you. Official and unofficial auditing is not permitted. Please see the Registrar’s Office (not the instructor) for all enrollment, registration, and auditing questions.

Course Description: A crisis can strike at any time, and it can have major impacts on a business, its reputation, and its customers. This course prepares future industry leaders to navigate crises. Each session dives into real-world case studies encompassing data breaches, product failures, regulatory incidents, service disruptions, cybersecurity attacks, and more. Through in-depth analysis and practical applications, students explore the multifaceted landscape of tech crises, crafting actionable crisis management plans. This course arms participants with a comprehensive playbook, honing their abilities to mitigate risks, lead during crises, and learn from incidents, ensuring preparedness and resilience in the ever-evolving tech sphere.
faculty_bio: Kathryn Guarini is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management and a Senior Fellow at Yale Engineering. She teaches and consults on technology, innovation, leadership, and crisis management in the technology industry. Her background includes serving as IBM’s global Chief Information Officer from 2021 to 2023, COO of IBM Research, and a research career in semiconductor technology. She holds a PhD and MS from Stanford University and a BS from Yale University, all in applied physics, and is a named inventor on more than 65 U.S. patents. Course Description:
Fixed income markets are among the largest in the world and fixed income products are a key component of any
investment strategy. This course covers the valuation and risk management of the key fixed income products –
bonds, futures, forwards, and swaps. It combines theory with practical examples demonstrating the complications
that arise when applying theory to realistic situations.

This course sets the foundation for options, derivatives, structured products and financial engineering covered in
MGT 900 (Fall-2 2026) and MGT 901 (Spring-2 2027).
faculty_bio: Saman Majd is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management. His teaching focuses on fixed-income markets, derivatives, and related financial instruments, including an advanced fixed-income markets course he taught at MIT Sloan. Before returning to academia, he held senior roles at Deutsche Asset Management and Salomon Brothers, including global leadership of derivatives and fixed-income government-bond trading. He previously taught finance at Wharton and Yale and holds a PhD and SM from MIT Sloan and a BA from Oxford. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/saman-majd))

Course Description: This course is designed to give you the tools to identify, understand, and evaluate tax planning opportunities. To maximize the lasting benefit you will get from this course, we begin by developing a conceptual framework for thinking about how tax rules affect business decisions. Once developed, the framework is brought to life by application to a variety of settings of particular interest to MBA students (e.g., investment, compensation planning, mergers and acquisitions). This course is helpful for students who plan to: 1. Work on Wall Street (e.g., Mergers & Acquisitions); 2. Do business consulting; 3. Do corporate tax planning; 4. Have some taxation knowledge.

Course Description:
This course examines the role of financial statement analysis in evaluating a firm’s financial performance and predicting its future economic condition. Topics include fundamental analysis and applications in both credit and equity markets. The course integrates accounting and finance into a practical framework for equity valuation, with particular emphasis on implications for IPOs, mergers and acquisitions, and equity investing. The course is designed to provide:
• Exposure to public sources of financial information used by capital market participants.
• Skills to critically analyze financial statements, SEC filings, and other disclosures.
• Insights into common accounting practices and potential earnings management techniques.
• Skills to assess and forecast a firm’s future economic condition.
• Experience applying financial information to a range of trading strategies.

Course Description: This course equips students with the core set of tools and strategies related to accounting and financial reporting from the perspective of a Chief Financial Officer at a private, entrepreneurial company. The class focus is on accounting-related financial metrics, financial reporting, and managerial accounting, with an emphasis on structuring accounting systems from the start-up phase through to exit. Students will gain a deep understanding of compliance with GAAP, tax considerations, and performance evaluation using accounting data. The course is based on the institutional setting that applies in the United States for both the entrepreneurial firm and key private capital market providers (private equity, venture capital, and angel investors).
Course Title: The Private Firm CFO: Accounting and Finance Strategies

Course Description: This course provides an introduction to the study of International Trade. The goal of the course is to teach you a set of conceptual tools that are useful for understanding what determines international trade and foreign investments. We will first review international trade theories that try to explain: Why do countries trade with each other? Do countries gain from trade? Who are the winners and losers? What goods should countries import and export? Can existing trade theories explain the rapid growth of China? Second, we will focus on foreign direct investment, multinational firms, and business opportunities in developing countries. For instance, we will explore what are the benefits and costs of hosting multinational companies in the developing world, both in the short- and long-run (in terms of productivity, living standards, culture, environmental effects). Third, we will analyze the role of trade policy. We will try to learn what are the trade and welfare effects of trade policy. This part of the course will review recent research that evaluates the effects of the trade war between China and the U.S. The course is self-contained. However, a background in micro and macroeconomics is desirable. For SOM students, the core is sufficient. You will get more out of the class if you often read the business section of a major newspaper (NYT, WDJ, FT, Economist, etc.).

Her research focuses on economic development, international trade, economic history, and the effects of foreign direct investment and trade in developing countries. She earned a PhD in Economics from UCLA in 2020 and previously was a postdoctoral associate at Princeton University’s International Economics Section. Originally from Costa Rica, she also holds a BSc from the Universidad de Costa Rica. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/diana-van-patten))

Course Description:
The art market is highly seductive, with its multibillion-dollar industry, hyped NFTs, sensational auctions, wealthy collectors, and lavish vernissages. Yet the reality is challenging. Nearly 30% of galleries operate at a loss, and over 90% of artists cannot make a living from their work. How can entrepreneurs succeed? Why does Gagosian generate over $1 billion in sales while the average gallery turns over only $200,000? What impact will Web3 have? Can new models replace auction houses and art fairs?
This course offers students firsthand insights into the art market through theoretical analysis and conversations with leading practitioners. Past speakers have included Jeff Koons, Jerry Saltz, Cecilia Alemani, and Noah Horowitz (CEO of Art Basel). Students will shape these sessions, challenge the experts, and develop their own perspectives. Fifteen places are reserved for artists from the Yale School of Art, creating a uniquely diverse and enriching classroom experience.
faculty_bio: Magnus Resch is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management, where he has taught since 2019. His research and teaching focus on the intersection of art, technology, and business, including the economics and entrepreneurship of the art market. He is an art-market expert, serial entrepreneur, and bestselling author of books including *How to Collect Art* and *How to Become a Successful Artist*. Resch holds a PhD in economics and has studied at Harvard, the London School of Economics, and the University of St. Gallen. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/magnus-resch))

Course Description: This course is designed to explore the ever-increasing impact of technology on our lives—as individuals, consumers, employees, managers, and policymakers. Technology has profoundly reshaped how we access information, interact with others, experience the world, and make decisions. Rather than focusing on the technical features of emerging tools, including, yes, Artificial Intelligence, the course examines the psychological and behavioral consequences of living in a technology-saturated environment. By developing an evidence-based and nuanced understanding of these issues, this course will enable more effective usage and management of technology.
faculty_bio: Gal Zauberman is the Joseph F. Cullman 3rd Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management. His research examines consumer judgment and decision-making, time perception, financial decision-making, the nature of experiences, and memory for emotions and choice. Course Description: Negotiating a job offer, founding a startup, resolving a dispute with a boss or coworker (or significant other) – negotiation skills will help you navigate all of these situations. This half-semester elective will hone your negotiation skills so that you can better negotiate with managers, investors, clients, coworkers, friends, and family. Each class session you will participate in real negotiation exercises with your peers. These exercises – paired with lectures, written reflections, and small group activities – will help you build a “toolkit” of negotiations skills and strategies that will make you more effective at creating and claiming value in your professional and personal life. This class covers both introductory and advanced topics; it assumes no prior experience with negotiation. Non-SOM students are welcome to enroll in the course.

Her research examines failure, recovery, and second chances, including how individuals, groups, and industries respond to setbacks and seek rehabilitation across contexts such as the military, scientific organizations, entertainment, and white-collar crime. She earned her PhD from Harvard Business School, completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Virginia, and previously served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/erin-l-frey))

Course Description: AM required.  AM student preregisted.  Open to other programs if space remains. Statistical Foundations is a practical, interactive course designed to equip students with the statistical tools necessary for modern financial data analysis. It provides a rigorous, hands-on exploration of advanced statistical methodologies, emphasizing regression techniques tailored for asset pricing research. Students will actively engage with complex financial phenomena throughout the course, using linear regression for prediction, inference, and other advanced topics. The course also introduces time series analysis and advanced estimation methods, such as Maximum Likelihood and Generalized Method of Moments, as crucial tools for aspiring financial analysts. Students are provided with ample opportunities to apply these tools to real-world financial data, using the statistical computing language R.
faculty_bio: Theis Ingerslev Jensen is an Assistant Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, where he has been a faculty member since fall 2023. His research focuses on empirical asset pricing, particularly using new datasets related to subjective expectations, with data-intensive projects that apply advanced statistical methods such as machine learning. Jensen grew up in Denmark and earned a PhD in Financial Economics from Copenhagen Business School in 2023. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/theis-ingerslev-jensen))

Course Description: Central banks which had historically operated in the background came to the forefront in the wake of the Global Financial Crisis of 2008/09, playing an increasingly critical, and increasingly visible, role in supporting growth and stability across countries, regions and the world. Although central banks around the world are broadly similar in terms of their mandates and policy instruments, emerging market central banks are different by way of the policy trade-offs they face, the degrees of freedom available to them and the environment in which they operate. As the global economic center of gravity shifts towards the emerging world, an intelligent appreciation of emerging economy perspectives is imperative for acquiring a broad-based worldview of the global economy. In that light, the course will focus on the challenges and dilemmas of central banking in emerging markets. Drawing from international, particularly emerging market experience of the last two decades, the course will prioritize practice over theory and breadth over depth. Although no quantitative models will be used, an understanding of the concepts of macroeconomics is a prerequisite.
Course Title: Emerging Market Central Banking and Financial Stability
faculty_bio: Sigríður “Sigga” Benediktsdóttir is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management and teaches part-time in its Master’s in Systemic Risk program. Her research focuses on international finance, particularly central banks and financial stability. She earned a PhD in economics from Yale in 2005 and has served as Director of the Financial Stability Department at the Central Bank of Iceland, an economist at the U.S. Federal Reserve Board, and an external expert for the IMF’s Financial Stability Assessment Program. She was also one of three members appointed to Iceland’s Parliamentary Special Investigation Commission on the causes of the 2008 banking collapse. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/sigridur-benediktsdottir))

Course Description:
Empirical work is the foundation of great economics. Theory is also the foundation of great
economics. Theorists work on closing the gap between theory and reality. Empiricists are
explorers that map the unchartered territory between theory and reality. This is a division
of labor view of Popper’s philosophy of science. This course is designed to help build a skill
set for pushing the empirical side of this proposition, particularly tailored to asset pricing
research. This is in large part a course in advanced statistical methods for finance. It is not a facts
course. I will bring in many empirical facts as we go. But the more important take-away for
you is a set of methods you can you to discover your own new facts.
faculty_bio: Bryan T. Kelly is the Frederick Frank ’54 and Mary C. Tanner Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, Associate Director of its International Center for Finance, a Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and head of machine learning at AQR Capital Management. His research focuses on asset pricing and financial econometrics, including financial machine learning, volatility and tail risk, systemic banking risk, financial intermediation, and financial networks. Course Description:
This course covers analytical tools and topics that have not been discussed in previous
operations doctoral courses at Yale SOM. The emphasis is on approaches to modeling
and analyzing operational processes across various application areas, including supply
chains, service operations, retail operations, platform operations, and sustainable
operations. Students will explore key ideas and methodologies established in the
literature of Operations Research and Operations Management, understand the contexts
in which certain conventions have been developed, and learn how to build effective
mathematical models.
faculty_bio: Zhen Lian is an Assistant Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management and a faculty fellow at Yale’s Center for Algorithms, Data, and Market Design. Her research focuses on optimization, transportation, public policy, and online marketplaces, particularly ridesharing and the gig economy. She teaches Operations Engine and Advanced Business Analytics, and previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Lyft on driver pay and incentive design. Lian holds a PhD from Cornell University and bachelor’s degrees from Peking University; she also helped redesign San Francisco school schedules, generating substantial transportation-cost savings. Course Description: This course equips students to use durable principles from economics, marketing, organizational behavior, accounting, and politics to achieve success in competitive environments.  Students will use course tools to understand a manager’s role in a company’s value creation and value capture activities.  Using this perspective, we will examine the potential for suppliers, buyers, complementors and traditional rivals to function as both competitors and cooperators to a company in the marketplace.    Emphasis will be placed on anticipating the actions of other marketplace participants by understanding those participants’ objectives and constraints.  The course explicitly recognizes that relevant players in the environment include governments, nonprofit organizations, and corporations and that all of these agents can behave both cooperatively and competitively.   Textbooks required for this course:  Microeconomics (Pindyck and Rubinfeld -whatever edition obtained for Economics is fine) and Coopetition (Brandenberger and Nalebuff).
faculty_bio: Kai Hao Yang is an Associate Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. His research uses mechanism design and information design to study privacy, algorithmic fairness, price discrimination, consumer data, online platforms, political economy, and finance; he also teaches economics courses at Yale SOM. He earned a B.A. in Political Science from National Taiwan University and an M.A. and Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Chicago, and was previously a postdoctoral associate at Yale’s Cowles Foundation. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kai-hao-yang))

Course Description: The course takes the viewpoint that the best way to create and keep a customer is to develop a deep understanding of customer behavior, integrate that understanding across the organization, and align the organizational structure to both satisfy current customer needs and adapt to changes in customer needs better than competitors. To be truly customer-focused and market-driven, a company (profit or nonprofit) should develop the capability to sense and respond to the changing needs of customers in the market. An important element of the course is the idea that customer focus must extend to the entire organization across all its major functions for it to be successful. The course consists of two main modules: (1) Understanding Customers and Creating a Superior Value Proposition and (2) Creating and Maintaining a Customer-Aligned Organization. The first module focuses on understanding customer needs in consumer and industrial markets from a multidisciplinary perspective (economics, psychology, and sociology) to create a superior value proposition; the second highlights how creating a customer-aligned organization requires functional perspectives that span marketing, operations, accounting, finance, and human resource management. Recommended Reading:  Marketing Management, 4/E, Russ Winer, New York University, Ravi Dhar, Yale University, ISBN-10: 0136074898, ISBN-13:  9780136074892
faculty_bio: Jiwoong Shin is a Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management and Senior Editor at *Marketing Science*. His research focuses on marketing strategy, applied economic theory, and digital markets, including advertising, pricing, targeting, customer relationship management, and AI-mediated competition. He holds a Ph.D. in Management Science from MIT and MS and BS degrees from Seoul National University, and his teaching has earned Yale’s Inspiring Yale Award. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jiwoong-shin))

Course Description: This course is about investors: what they do, how they think, and what they care about. The course is, in places, quantitative. Course topics include returns, risk, and prices; asset allocation; efficient markets; valuation and fundamentals-based investing; the capital asset pricing model (CAPM); quantitative equity investing; bond markets; evaluating money manager performance; futures and options; and investment errors and human psychology.
faculty_bio: Stefano Giglio is the Frederic D. Wolfe Professor of Finance, Management, and Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management. His research focuses on asset pricing, macroeconomics, and climate finance, particularly ways to hedge crash, uncertainty, and climate risks. He teaches finance, including courses related to asset management and climate finance. Before joining Yale, he was an associate professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and earned his PhD in economics from Harvard University. Course Description: Firms need governments to protect property rights, enforce contracts, mitigate market failures, and maintain an environment that is conducive to doing business. Governments depend on the private sector for investment, employment, and revenue, and sometimes to mitigate political failures. Future managers and leaders of both for-profit and non-profit private sector entities must understand the ways in which their organization’s mission is dependent on government and devise appropriate strategies vis-à-vis the public sector. Conversely, future public sector leaders must be cognizant of the effects of government action on business. This course is designed to expose students to frameworks derived primarily from the fields of economics and political science that help us analyze the social and political environments within which business operates. The first half of the course focuses on analyzing how government institutions affect the conduct of business and how business can shape government and policy. The second half does deeper dives into a number of pressing policy issues (such as gender and racial discrimination, immigration policy, education policy, public health in light of the COVID-19 epidemic, and the role of evidence in policymaking) that have large effects on employees, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders. Beyond political science and economics, a rigorous analysis of these topics will require us to also draw on scholarship from the fields of law, history and sociology.
faculty_bio: Mushfiq Mobarak is the Jerome Kasoff ’54 Professor of Management and Economics at Yale School of Management, with a joint appointment in Yale’s Department of Economics. He is a development economist whose research uses field experiments to study how people in developing countries adopt welfare-improving technologies and behaviors, as well as how effective interventions can be scaled. He founded and directs the Yale Research Initiative on Innovation and Scale (Y-RISE), and teaches State & Society and Development Economics. His previous affiliations include the World Bank, IMF, Innovations for Poverty Action, J-PAL at MIT, and the International Growth Centre at LSE. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/ahmed-mushfiq-mobarak))

Launched in 2008 at the Yale School of Management, the Global Social Entrepreneurship (GSE) India course links teams of Yale students with social enterprises based in India. GSE is committed to channeling the skills of Yale students to assist Indian organizations to expand their reach and impact on “base of the pyramid” communities. Yale students partner with mission-driven social entrepreneurs (SEs) to focus on a specific management challenge that the student/SE teams work together to address during the semester.  GSE has worked with more than 50 leading and emerging Indian social enterprises engaged in economic development, sustainable energy, women’s empowerment, education, environmental conservation, and affordable housing. The course covers both theoretical and practical issues, including case studies and discussions on social enterprise, developing a theory of change and related social metrics, financing social businesses, the role of civil society in India, framing a consulting engagement, managing team dynamics, etc. The course will be taught by Asha Ghosh, Lecturer at SOM. The course meets on Wednesday afternoons 2:40 – 5:40 during Fall-2 and Spring-1. Students will travel to India to work on-site with their partner SEs, and for a convening of all the student/SE project teams, in mid- to late January 2026 for 10 days. As with the International Experience and the Global Network Immersion Week, students will be responsible for covering the costs of their round-trip airfare to India and related expenses (such as visa and immunizations). Course Description: Business is an activity in which parties exchange goods or services for valuable consideration. The goal of this course is to examine the ethical dimensions of such activities and develop skills for identifying and weighting ethical considerations. The aims are twofold. One, we will discover the tools we use for reasoning about right and wrong at the individual, firm, and policy levels. Discussion and debate about the readings, including on Canvas forums, are a frequent part of the course. Two, we will explore “blind spots” – reasons why people fail to see the ethical dimension of decisions and thus, how they fail to live up to their own ethical standards.

Course Description:
Please note that full attendance in the first and last classes are required to get credit for the course. Additionally, please note that there will be an assignment due prior to the first class. Auditing is not permitted.

Finance can be likened to the circulatory system of the global economy, and we will focus on the past, present and future of that system. The course is designed to deal with questions such as these: What is the global financial system and how does it work? What are the pressures on that system including market, regulatory, political and social dynamics? What are the key challenges to that system? How can the system be strengthened? In this course we are defining the global financial system (GFS) as encompassing central banks, commercial banks, and other financial institutions such as asset managers and private equity firms, financial regulators and international organizations. Thus, we will encompass subjects such as the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, Goldman Sachs and the Hong Kong Shanghai Bank, the Carlyle Group and the BlackRock Investment Management Co., the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Financial Stability Board, the Bank for International Settlements and the International Monetary Fund. We will take a broad view of the GFS including its history, its geopolitical framework, its economic foundations and its legal underpinnings. We will consider the GFS as a critical public good in the same way that clean air is a public good. We will look at a number of other key issues such as how the GFS deals with economic growth, economic and financial stability, distributional questions, employment issues, and long-term investments in infrastructure. We will discuss how new technologies are affecting several of the biggest issues in global finance. We will examine the GFS as a large-scale complex network, thereby compelling us to see it in an interconnected and multidisciplinary way. The emphasis will be on the practice of global finance more than the theory.

Course Description:
Most of the attention to issues of financial stability focuses on the role of the central bank and prudential regulators in preventing the failure of systemically important financial institutions. As we’ve learned through the experience of the Global Financial Crisis of 2008 (GFC), as well as the regional bank failures in the United States and the failure of Credit Suisse in Switzerland in the spring of 2023, preventive efforts are not always successful.
The capability of public authorities to manage the orderly failure of systemically important financial institutions, without resort to public support on an open institution basis – in other words, a bailout that protects the shareholders, creditors, and management of the institution – has been a goal of the United States and the international community since the 2008 Crisis. The failure of public authorities to have this capability increases the risk of financial crises and erodes public trust and support for preventive efforts. It also creates an unlevel playing field in favor of institutions that are deemed “too big to fail” and long-run market expectations and moral hazard that lay the groundwork for future financial system instability.
The purpose of this course is to review the work on systemic resolution that has been done, both in the United States and internationally, since the 2008 Crisis to develop the capability of public authorities to manage the orderly failure of systemically important banks, both global (GSIBs) and domestic (DSIBs). It will consider the financial stability, accountability, competition, and moral hazard trade-offs between open institution support and resolution and the difficult choices policymakers have to make.

Gruenberg previously chaired the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and held leadership roles with the International Association of Deposit Insurers, the Financial Stability Board, and the Financial Stability Oversight Council; he earned a J.D. from Case Western Reserve Law School and an A.B. from Princeton University. Course Description:
This course explores the history of finance through direct engagement with primary objects — clay tablets, coins, bonds, banknotes, securities, and artworks — held in Yale's extraordinary collections. Each week, students meet in a different Yale collection under the guidance of expert curators to examine objects that document the invention and evolution of financial instruments, institutions, and markets from antiquity to the modern era.
The course traces several interlocking themes: the emergence of debt and credit in ancient Mesopotamia; the invention and diffusion of coinage; the development of sovereign debt, corporate securities, and paper money in early-modern Europe and China; the global expansion of finance through trading companies and colonial enterprise; and the material culture of money in Africa and the Americas. By working directly with original objects, students develop a tactile understanding of financial innovation that no textbook can replicate — and confront the physical, legal, and artistic dimensions of instruments that are today entirely digital.
 
Learning Objectives
1.	Understand the deep history of financial instruments and institutions through primary material evidence
2.	Develop the ability to "read" financial objects — contracts, coins, bonds, banknotes, artworks — as sources of economic information
3.	Trace the co-evolution of financial innovation, legal institutions, and political authority across civilizations
4.	Appreciate the global diffusion of financial technology and the role of cultural exchange in shaping markets

Course Description:
Artificial Intelligence  is a transformative force across the financial services industry, reshaping both traditional finance firms and the fast-growing fintech landscape. Its applications grow rapidly from fraud detection, algorithmic trading to AI-based personalized financial advisory, and risk management, enhancing operational efficiency, accuracy, and strategic competitiveness.

Unlike past technologies, AI (particularly the latest generation of Generative and Agentic Models) impacts the core of financial business models. It is driving a shift from traditional finance firms toward fully digital, AI-driven providers, with far-reaching implications for business models, workforce dynamics, and the future of finance careers..

This course explores the innovative application of AI in the financial sector, focusing on the technological foundations and strategic use cases shaping its future. It examines the key challenges and opportunities in developing and deploying next-generation AI solutions, including both intrapreneurial initiatives within existing firms and new venture creation. Each week covers a core AI-in-finance topic, integrating business impact with technical depth, while addressing regulatory and business considerations.

Course Description:
In today’s AI-driven organizations, the real advantage isn’t just knowing how to use tools -- it’s knowing how to structure decisions. This course teaches you how to translate messy business problems into clear objectives, constraints, and tradeoffs that can be rigorously evaluated. Rather than focusing primarily on predictive modeling, we focus on deciding what to do: allocating resources, designing operations, and stress-testing strategy under uncertainty. You’ll build hands-on decision models using spreadsheet, optimization, simulation, and coding-based tools, but the real skill you’ll gain is structured thinking that applies across consulting, product, operations, and entrepreneurship.

In the first half of the course, we will review and extend quantitative tools surveyed in the MBA core course MGT 405, greatly expanding the range of business problems that can be solved using existing methods. In the second half of the course, we will introduce simulation modeling, a useful tool for guiding decisions under uncertainty. Modeling concepts covered include linear programming, network optimization, integer programming, nonlinear optimization methods, Monte Carlo simulation, estimating summary statistics using simulation, and evaluating accuracy and precision in simulation models.

The first half of the course will be taught primarily in Excel with the Solver Add-In. The second half of the course will use R and/or Python as modeling environments, with emphasis on understanding, adapting, validating, and communicating model-based analysis rather than on prior programming experience. We will also examine how AI tools can support analytics workflows, including code generation, debugging, documentation, and model critique, while emphasizing the human judgment required to verify assumptions, interpret results, and make defensible business decisions.

There are no prerequisites for this course; you do not need to be familiar with coding to take this course.
Course Title: Analytics in the Age of AI

Her research focuses on optimization, transportation, public policy, and online marketplaces, particularly ridesharing and the gig economy. She teaches Operations Engine and Advanced Business Analytics, and previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Lyft on driver pay and incentive design. Lian holds a PhD from Cornell University and bachelor’s degrees from Peking University; she also helped redesign San Francisco school schedules, generating substantial transportation-cost savings. Course Description: One day, you’ll lead something—perhaps a team, a company, or an enterprise entirely your own. When that day comes, every decision you make about people, policy, capital, or organizational culture will reflect deeper beliefs about what really matters. This course helps you understand and test those beliefs. Is the goal to maximize economic value? To create value for all stakeholders? Balance purpose and profit? Build something that endures? Or something else entirely? Your own thoughts about such beliefs will be stretched and challenged as complexity builds throughout the course—short-term demands against longer time horizons, competing interests and pressures, unexpected developments. Through direct conversations with CEOs and real-world examples, we’ll examine and debate how leaders navigate these complexities, and what they rely on to guide decisions and build enduring organizations. Ultimately, you’ll form your own view of what you're optimizing for when you're in charge.

Course Description:
Due to the hands-on nature of this course, we strictly require class attendance and participation. This course is a highly practical course that puts students in the seat of the private equity investor evaluating a live investment opportunity. It is co-instructed by Professor Song Ma, Professor of Finance and Entrepreneurship, and Mr. James Soldano, Managing Partner, Sterling Investment Partners.

Working in 4–5 person deal teams, students follow a single transaction from initial due diligence through final bid, learning to assess an opportunity through business, commercial, and financial due diligence; negotiate and structure the financing; design performance-oriented management incentives; negotiate a purchase agreement; and present a fully vetted recommendation—with a proposed valuation—to an investment committee composed of the instructors and TAs. Weekly lectures reinforce each stage of the deal lifecycle, culminating in a team IC presentation.

Alongside the deal itself, students will learn how to leverage AI to enhance the efficiency and quality of due diligence, “stress test” an investment thesis and financial modeling assumptions, and to review legal agreements, including credit term sheets and the purchase agreement. The goal is not just to evaluate a deal but to learn how AI is reshaping the private equity investor's workflow. 
Prerequisites: MBA students must have earned at least a PR grade in both Investor and Sourcing and Managing Funds. Students enrolled in other programs must demonstrate proficiency in equivalent coursework covering both investments and corporate finance.

([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) His research focuses on innovation economics, entrepreneurship, financial economics, artificial intelligence, and big data, with additional work in corporate strategy, antitrust, labor, and business law. Student teams will prepare investment materials based on transaction case studies which mirror a PE firm’s process of evaluating LBO opportunities.

Course Description: This half semester course will provide an introduction to real estate development, investment, finance and strategy outside of the United States.  Global investment in financial assets, the need for risk diversification, the increased accuracy of property records, greater transparency, more relaxed laws permitting foreign investment, and population movement around the world—all of these trends have led to a tremendous increase in cross-border real estate investing for both private equity and public companies.  While many studies of international real estate focus on the role of foreign real property in the U. S. institutional portfolio, this course will take a wider and more historical view of the cultural attitudes towards real estate around the world and how they impact the quality and risk of investment assets.  Detailed analysis will begin with property level due diligence in order to provide a fundamental understanding of how and why property markets differ by country beyond simple supply/demand dynamics.  This course will consist of three parts:  a.) a micro-market analysis of real property characteristics in various countries around the world, including financing, leasing and valuation; b.) an analysis of investment vehicles—public and private—available to institutional investors, as well as cross-border transactions, and c.) a macro-market view of world space and capital  markets, the rationale for international investing, trends in capital flows and portfolio composition and the various ways in which risk is measured and mitigated.  Each part of the course will require a brief individual assignment completed over a two-week period.  The first research project will be a study of a significant real property asset outside of the United States, including its market, ownership, legal structure, valuation, and transaction history.  Both the G-8 and G-20 nations will be the object of study, but individual students are free to concentrate on any country of interest.  The second research project will consist of an analysis of a private equity or publicly-traded foreign property company, its current fair value, competitive advantage and future prospects.  An interview with a top executive of a company will be encouraged and facilitated.  The third research project will consist of a comparative analysis of world property markets and the hypothetical investment in a portfolio of real estate assets across three or more foreign property markets.  The course will consist of lectures, discussion, case studies and readings on international real estate from a variety of sources.  No final exam or group project will be required.
faculty_bio: Kevin D. Gray is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale University and principal of Kevin D. Gray Consulting, a real estate advisory firm. Course Description:
The course is designed to introduce the challenges and pitfalls of financing new enterprises. The course primarily takes the perspective of an entrepreneur. Broadly speaking, entrepreneurial financing decisions have a life cycle. The cycle begins with identifying opportunities, moves to marshaling resources to take advantage of these opportunities and executing the business plan, and ends with harvesting the venture's success. Accordingly, the course has three sections: Identifying and Valuing Opportunities, Structuring Deals, and Harvesting Opportunities.

Increasingly, the entrepreneur does not work alone. This course pays particular attention to how artificial intelligence and autonomous agents are reshaping the way founders raise, structure, and manage capital across this life cycle. We consider how a founder might delegate to specialized agents—a market-and-opportunity scout, a valuation and modeling analyst, a deal-structuring and term-sheet advisor, an investor-relations coordinator—and what the founder must still own: judgment, relationships, and the strategic decisions that cannot be automated away.

This course combines lectures and case studies. The lecture part will equip students with important techniques in each stage of entrepreneurial finance, as well as the skills to deploy and supervise the AI tools and agents that apply these techniques at speed and scale. Those techniques are applied to case studies covering interesting entrepreneurial areas such as IT, healthcare, the sharing economy, and impact investment, with attention to how an agent-augmented founder would approach each situation differently from a traditional one.

Course Description:
This course develops the theoretical foundations and economic intuition of modern asset pricing, organized around a
single unifying idea: the stochastic discount factor (SDF). Beginning with preferences, expected utility, and portfolio
choice, we show how the law of one price and the absence of arbitrage lead to a fundamental pricing relation, and how
essentially every asset pricing model amounts to a different theory of the discount factor. Within this framework we
treat state prices, complete and incomplete markets, and risk-neutral pricing, and we revisit the classic mean–variance
and CAPM results as special cases rather than as starting points. We then turn to consumption-based and equilibrium
models that tie risk premia to the macroeconomy, along with the risk-sharing and Pareto-optimality ideas behind them.
Throughout, the emphasis is on the economics governing the level and dynamics of asset prices.

Course Description: Financial markets play an important role in driving macroeconomic outcomes. Conversely, macroeconomic stabilization policy has become increasingly central to understanding asset prices. This course explores the rich set of interactions between financial markets, business cycles, and macroeconomic policy. We develop a framework for how asset prices and other shocks drive business cycles, and how central banks influence interest rates and asset prices to stabilize output and inflation. We also touch on other stabilization policies, including quantitative easing and financial-crisis interventions. We apply the framework to recent events—the Great Recession, the Covid-19 recession and recovery, the resurgence of inflation, bank runs, and the effects of tariffs and energy shocks on markets and policy. The course suits anyone seeking a macroeconomic perspective on financial markets.

Course Description:
This course presents an introduction to asset pricing at the PhD level. The first half of the
course covers the theory of choice under uncertainty, then develops classical asset pricing
theory in discrete time, including the principle of no arbitrage, mean-variance analysis,
the CAPM, and factor models. The second half of the course will focus on the connection
between asset prices and macroeconomic quantities. After covering the main models
based on consumption data, we will move to production-based asset pricing and pricing
in the presence of various frictions. We will also cover optimal (short-run and especially
long-run) portfolio choice.
The course assumes knowledge of microeconomics and statistics at an advanced
undergraduate level, but does not require any prior knowledge of finance. It is aimed at
first-year PhD students in Financial Economics.

Course Description: This course is designed to provide students with a set of practical but powerful statistical methods valuable across a range of professional and personal settings. We being with data structure, sampling methodologies and data quality, then introduce advanced tools such as nonparametric regression and density estimation, quantile regression, maximum likelihood estimation and limited dependent variable models. Finally, we turn to causal inference: many of the most important questions in business, public policy and beyond often revolve around understanding how some variable X affects some other variable Y (e.g., how does demand for my product respond to a change in price; does microfinance reduce poverty; will drinking a glass of wine a day affect my life expectancy). We examine when and how data can be used to infer causality, using techniques such as regression discontinuity designs, matching estimators, instrumental variables, synthetic controls, differences-in-differences (...-in differences), event studies, randomized controlled trials and A/B testing. The emphasis will be on understanding the underlying concepts, and the practical use, implications and limitations of these techniques.

Course Description:
Attendance is required for the first two classes to retain a place in the course or on the waiting list. This course has a mandatory weekly lab meeting and a mandatory off-campus weekend retreat (see important dates for the 2025-2026 academic calendar at https://faculty.som.yale.edu/heidibrooks/interpersonal-and-group-dynamics/). 
Amidst an epidemic of loneliness and rising levels of burnout—often fueled by interpersonal stressors at work—our capacity to build meaningful connections is essential. Studies have shown that the average manager spends about two-thirds of their time interacting with others. It should be no surprise that skill in interpersonal relationships is one of the most frequent determinants of managerial success or failure. This course is designed to help students learn some of the skills necessary for successfully navigating and leading in the face of fast-paced, complex human interaction. The central focus is to increase students' ability to understand and diagnose interpersonal dynamics as well as to increase personal understanding of how they impact others.
This course is a memory-making, powerful and even transformational experience for many students. While readings and group exercises are used to begin discussion, the core learning material emerges in small group interaction. Students learn how they function in small groups and how they relate to others from feedback and reaction of other class members. As such, students planning to enroll should understand that the course methodologies are likely quite different than most courses you have taken to date. Much of the learning will emerge from a) personal reflection on interpersonal and group dynamics and b) the ability/willingness to learn interpersonally from experience, risk-taking, self-disclosure, and feedback.
Interested students are encouraged to attend the first session to better understand this unique course experience.  Attendance is required for the first two classes to retain a place in the course or on the waiting list. Note that the first assignment requires screening for this course. Course Description: This is a semester long course that provides an examination of current theory, research and policy on urban poverty and regional economic development in the U.S., as a background for economic development interventions in city and community settings. The course topics include: (1) measurements and theoretical explanations of poverty, incorporating both panel data and ethnography; (2) analytic tools for assessing community and regional economic flows; and (3) strategies for economic development and wealth building in urban populations and communities. We examine innovative approaches in the traditional areas of economic development practice including: strategies for revitalizing the regional economic base, business creation and development, workforce development and skills training, housing, education, and financial services. Strategies we explore include: cluster based economic development, place-based anchor strategies, sectoral workforce development training, affordable housing and community land trusts, neighborhood revitalization, and business development. By the end of the semester, students will: 1. Develop an understanding of the portfolio of theories, tools and strategies for regional economic development for urban regions in United States; 2. Build technical skills to analyze the economic base of a regional economy and apply these skills to a region of their choosing; 3. Build technical skills to analyze the demographic base of a regional economy and apply these skills to a region of their choosing; 4. Develop an understanding of the historic forces shaping the current material conditions of unequal economic development across regional geographies and demographic groups as it relates to particular regions of the U.S. metropole; 5. Critically evaluate a range of approaches to economic development (informed by learning goals 1-4) and analyze their utility for a specific region; 6. Design a communication tool using two formats (Ted talk, opED) to showcase an innovative approach to economic development exploring its potential for application in a specific US context.

At other times, while life or death may not be at stake, a leader must still decide difficult issues: when to partner with unsavory characters, when to admit failure, when to release information or make choices transparent. The pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and continued instability around the world all make clearer than ever the consequences of decisions in one community that can affect the entire world. This interdisciplinary seminar draws on perspectives from law, management, and public policy in exploring how leaders develop their principles, respond when their principles fail or conflict, and make real-world choices when, in fact, there are no good choices.
