Course Description: Around the world, households and the small enterprises they run (the self-employed, family businesses, gig workers, smallholder farmers) face significant risks to their incomes, as well as challenges in growing them. Insurance, credit and other financial services are designed to address these issues, but in many cases the markets for these instruments may be incomplete or missing, particularly for the least well-off or in marginalized communities. This course studies the nature of risk and the demand for financial services among households and small enterprises in both developed and developing economies; the role of financial instruments in addressing those needs; the reasons why these markets may fail; and potential solutions, from market design to public policy. Throughout, we pay attention to the different forms these instruments may take and the different potential providers, including the commercial market, informal institutions, social arrangements, nonprofits and the state. The emphasis will be on the household and small enterprise as a single economic unit (how ordinary people manage everyday risk and finance their livelihoods, including access to capital for starting or growing a small business) rather than on personal financial planning, the financing of large or high-growth ventures, corporate hedging or system-level finance. Throughout, we will draw on economic theory and empirical evidence.
Course Title: Risk, Insurance and Finance for Households and Small Enterprises

Course Description:
The purpose of this class is to teach you how to evaluate public policies. This will help you:
a) Understand what political viewpoints are most reasonable in light of the existing evidence
b) Constructively discuss public policy

The course will emphasize two perspectives:
1) Cost-benefit analysis – how can we quantitatively determine the costs and benefits of a given policy by determining who is impacted and valuing those impacts?
2) Economic theory – when do markets work well? When might public provision be better?

Questions covered will include (among others):
Public transit systems help people travel more quickly, but they cost a lot of money. How should we evaluate if this cost if worthwhile?
A carbon tax would harm consumers today by making goods more expensive; this burden would be highest for low-income households who spend a larger percentage of income on emission-intensive goods. It would also reduce carbon emissions and combat global warming. Should we do it?
Most OECD countries have publicly provided healthcare. In Medicare Parts C/D and the Affordable Care Act, the US is moving increasingly towards a system of privately provided care with government subsidies. Should people under the age of 65 be allowed to buy into Medicare?
Should we have school vouchers which allow parents to use public funding to choose amongst local and non-local public schools, as well as private or charter schools?
Unemployment insurance provides an income stream for people who lose their job. But evidence shows that people find work faster when unemployment insurance is less generous. How generous should UI be?
Should we replace the social safety net with a system in which every single person receives $12,000 in cash whether or not they are currently working?
Should we replace the current social security program with individual savings accounts?
What is the role of AI in public policy?

Course Description: This course will discuss the economics of healthcare markets with a focus on understanding what is inefficient, what reforms and innovations might make things better and how strategic interactions among firms impact profits, health outcomes, and social welfare. Topics covered will include: measuring the value of health and medical care; the efficiency of US healthcare relative to other countries with different modes of delivery; the role of health insurance and competition among insurers; assessing healthcare delivery facilities such as hospitals and nursing homes; the healthcare workforce and physician behavior; pharmaceutical and medical device innovation; lessons from behavioral economics about the role of imperfectly informed consumers; the impact of the Affordable Care Act on health care in the US; and the role of AI in healthcare.
